record.title: OpenMAS-GCom reports controlled diagnosis of multi-agent system components
record.summary: An arXiv paper introduces OpenMAS-GCom, a benchmark that compares multi-agent configurations with one component changed while tasks, models, prompts and budget limits are held fixed. The paper reports 17 configurations across 29 datasets in six domains, four interventions, and 400 frozen multi-document tasks requiring source-aware conflict resolution. In a five-dataset aggregate, it reports a 3.58 percentage-point mean score loss after specialist removal versus 0.58 points after critic removal. These are author-reported benchmark results; independent reproduction and broader task-weighted interpretation remain open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a controlled benchmark that changes one organizational component at a time while keeping task inputs, models, prompts and computation-budget limits fixed. It evaluates 17 configurations across 29 datasets in six domains and four intervention families: graph rewiring, role removal, incorrect-message injection and worker failure.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five datasets, the paper reports mean score falling by 3.58 percentage points after removing specialists and by 0.58 points after removing critics; it also reports exceptions and differing response to incorrect messages across configurations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report adding 400 frozen multi-document tasks with cross-document dependencies, conflicting records and structured answers requiring source identifiers. On these tasks, different configurations lead in strict exact-match accuracy and accuracy per token.

evidence_gaps.description: The multi-agent component-removal and message-corruption results have not been independently reproduced in this review.
An accessible benchmark implementation and exact tested configuration artifacts were not located and inspected during this activation.
External validity of the 29 datasets and constructed 400-task suite for deployed multi-agent workloads is unestablished.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper’s interventions and benchmark findings hold, they can change how teams diagnose role and communication choices in multi-agent systems; the results remain bounded to the paper’s tested configurations and task suites.
limitations: All quantitative findings are author-reported; this activation did not run the benchmark or independently reproduce the reported comparisons.

The five-dataset aggregate for specialist and critic removal does not establish that the same effect holds across every dataset, task mix, model or production setting; the paper itself reports task/configuration-specific differences.
The authors describe an open-sourced benchmark library, but this activation did not locate and inspect a reproducible code artifact.
The G-MAS-Complex benchmark has 400 frozen constructed tasks; the paper does not establish external validity for real-world production workloads.
brief.summary: An arXiv paper introduces OpenMAS-GCom, a benchmark that compares multi-agent configurations with one component changed while tasks, models, prompts and budget limits are held fixed. The paper reports 17 configurations across 29 datasets in six domains, four interventions, and 400 frozen multi-document tasks requiring source-aware conflict resolution. In a five-dataset aggregate, it reports a 3.58 percentage-point mean score loss after specialist removal versus 0.58 points after critic removal. These are author-reported benchmark results; independent reproduction and broader task-weighted interpretation remain open.

technical.claimed_result: Across five datasets, authors report mean loss of 3.58 points after specialist removal and 0.58 after critic removal, with configuration-dependent message-corruption and worker-failure effects. The 400-task G-MAS-Complex suite produces different leaders for strict accuracy and accuracy per token.
technical.compute_or_cost: The benchmark records token usage, calls, latency, executed nodes/edges and retries. This activation did not independently measure run cost; paper tables report configuration-dependent accuracy per token.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary paper provides a specific benchmark design and quantitative author-reported intervention results. the research desk did not independently verify those outcomes.
technical.mechanism: Represent a multi-agent system by collaboration units, communication links, shared intermediate information and execution rules; compare an original run to a paired version with one graph, role, message or worker component changed while common task/model/prompt/budget settings are held fixed.
technical.novelty: Intervention-based attribution of communication, role, message and worker effects under fixed controls, paired with multi-document conflict/provenance tasks; this extends final-score-only comparison with explicit component-diagnosis claims.
technical.regime: 17 single-agent, ordinary multi-agent and graph-enhanced configurations; 29 datasets in six domains; 400 frozen multi-document tasks; matched controls as described in the paper. Findings remain author-reported and benchmark-specific.
technical.reproducibility: arXiv HTML contains the design, controls and run-record schema. Although the authors describe a reusable open benchmark library, this activation did not inspect a public implementation or rerun results.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, each intervention is paired against the original configuration with the same task set, model/backend, prompts, parser and budget controls; no independent benchmark comparison was performed here.

brief.title: OpenMAS-GCom reports controlled diagnosis of multi-agent system components
brief.why_it_matters: Final scores alone can hide which collaboration component contributes to performance. If the reported controlled comparisons hold, this benchmark offers a way to test whether roles, communication and worker availability matter under fixed task/model settings, informing multi-agent architecture and evaluation choices. The results do not establish that specialists are universally necessary or that the paper’s aggregates transfer to production systems.
